recent_posts.title: Getting AI from Handy to Heartfelt -- Fatbobman's Swift Weekly #134
recent_posts.summary: A Swift-focused weekly newsletter covering AI-assisted development workflows, Swift concurrency fundamentals (including Task.immediate in Swift 6.2, protocol design in Swift 6), Xcode project automation with Tuist and XcodeGen, SwiftUI appearance mode switching, a six-year watchOS mapping journey, and two new tools: Kadr (a Swift DSL for video composition using AVFoundation) and SwiftVLC (a modern libVLC wrapper for SwiftUI). The editorial also reflects on using AI tools with custom documentation to steer code generation toward a personal SwiftUI state pattern.

recent_posts.title: Swift Concurrency is Gaining Broader Adoption -- Fatbobman's Swift Weekly #133
recent_posts.summary: Swift concurrency adoption is accelerating as the ecosystem matures, with developers increasingly migrating legacy projects to the new model. The newsletter covers several topics: debugging flaky tests caused by executor context misunderstandings, the distinction between structured (async let, TaskGroup) and unstructured (Task) concurrency, a SwiftUI .refreshable pitfall where state updates cancel the refresh task, Swift 6.3's experimentalCGen feature enabling native C code generation in SwiftPM, a case study of migrating 300 screens to SwiftUI using a UIKit-backed navigation strategy, Mini Swift (a C-written Swift compiler targeting WASM), and Yotei (a SwiftUI calendar component library).

recent_posts.title: From OpenSwiftUI to DanceUI: A Different Way to Dive into SwiftUI -- Fatbobman's Swift Weekly #132
recent_posts.summary: ByteDance has open-sourced DanceUI, a SwiftUI replication project that has already been used in production within some ByteDance product modules. Alongside the existing OpenSwiftUI community project, DanceUI offers developers another lens for understanding SwiftUI's internal mechanisms — dependency graphs, runtime behavior, and host integration. The newsletter also covers: applying the Interface Segregation Principle to avoid bloated protocols in iOS, animating strikethroughs in SwiftUI Text using the TextRenderer API (iOS 17+), using SwiftUI Previews for accessibility validation, lessons from a UIKit-to-SwiftUI migration, how to properly cancel in-flight repeatForever animations, a solo developer building ~300 Swift packages, a custom AST-based Swift linting tool, and the Swift Craft 2026 conference in the UK.

recent_posts.title: How vibe coding is dismantling software copyright and what developers can do about it
recent_posts.summary: AI-powered vibe coding is eroding traditional software copyright protections from multiple angles: the bar for establishing code ownership has risen, proving infringement is harder, and functional cloning has become trivially easy. A Reddit incident exposed a developer who used AI to repackage Paul Hudson's open-source Ignite framework with minimal changes, while a macOS app was pixel-for-pixel cloned shortly after launch. China's copyright authority now requires notarized declarations that no AI was used in code development, and European/US case law is trending similarly. The newsletter argues that developers' true moat going forward is community trust and maker credibility, not code secrecy. Also covered: the Swift Blog Carnival on 'Tiny Languages', SwiftUI menu selection patterns, List alternatives using Container View API, exposing AppIntents as MCP tools, interactive WidgetKit widgets, and iOS/macOS file storage with iCloud.

recent_posts.title: Apple's Rare Concession: When Critical Vulnerabilities Meet the 'Update Refusal' Wave -- Fatbobman's Swift Weekly #130
recent_posts.summary: A Swift developer newsletter covering two major iOS security threats (Coruna and DarkSword) that exploited watering hole attacks across iOS 13–18.7, prompting Apple's rare decision to backport security patches to iOS 18 via iOS 18.7.7. The update refusal wave, driven by iOS 26's Liquid Glass redesign and UK age verification requirements, left millions of devices vulnerable. The issue also curates SwiftUI animation internals via the Animatable protocol, SPM localization resource sharing across modules, a Coordinator-based navigation pattern, AI agent workflows for large dev teams, and a book on SwiftUI architecture patterns.

recent_posts.title: A Wall Away, Worlds Apart -- Fatbobman's Swift Weekly #129
recent_posts.summary: Issue #129 of Fatbobman's Swift Weekly covers the Let's Vision conference in Shanghai, where the author reflects on the tension between AI-driven efficiency and developer craftsmanship. Key recommendations include the Swift 6.3 release (focused on concurrency, C++ interoperability, and cross-platform progress), a type-driven JSONValue approach for unstable APIs, a six-part series on building native AI agents in Swift, insights from Apple's Liquid Glass design workshop, and a major App Store Connect update with 100+ new metrics. Additional items cover Package Traits in Xcode 26.4, perceived performance techniques in SwiftUI, the new lineHeight modifier in iOS 26, and Cove, an open-source Swift 6 macOS database client.

recent_posts.title: An Attempt to Make Core Data Feel More Like Modern Swift
recent_posts.summary: Core Data Evolution (CDE) is an experimental Swift library that modernizes Core Data development without replacing it. It introduces SwiftData-style macro-based model declarations via @PersistentModel, type-safe predicate building with TypedPath (supporting persistent name aliasing), actor-based concurrency isolation via @NSModelActor, and improved testing utilities including runtime schema generation and per-test SQLite stores. CDE keeps .xcdatamodeld as the production model source while adding a modern Swift expression layer on top. A companion CLI tool (cde-tool) handles code generation, validation, and alignment between model files and source declarations. The project also integrates with PersistentHistoryTrackingKit and iCloudSyncStatusKit for a complete modern Core Data stack.

recent_posts.title: Apple at 50 and Me at 51 -- Fatbobman's Swift Weekly #127
recent_posts.summary: A Swift developer newsletter covering Apple's 50th anniversary, a reflection on Core Data's continued relevance in 2026, pitfalls when migrating from GCD to Swift Concurrency, a nine-step framework for selecting AI agent skills, a JetBrains survey targeting Swift developers, and tools including DataStoreKit (a custom SwiftData SQLite backend) and Playwright bindings for Swift.

recent_posts.title: Why I'm Still Thinking About Core Data in 2026
recent_posts.summary: Core Data remains in active use in 2026 despite being 21 years old, but it increasingly clashes with modern Swift idioms. Three core pain points are identified: the model layer's expressiveness lags behind modern Swift (NSManagedObject carries heavy Objective-C legacy), the concurrency model is stuck in the GCD era with unsafe patterns and nested perform closures, and the tension between flexibility, type safety, and schema drift grows as projects evolve. The author argues that experience-based workarounds are no longer sufficient, especially as AI-assisted coding generates generic patterns rather than project-specific conventions. The proposed solution is an open-source library called CoreDataEvolution, which uses Swift Macros to modernize model declarations, introduces SwiftData-style actor isolation, improves type safety in predicates and sort descriptors, and provides a CLI tool to keep source declarations aligned with the Core Data model — all without replacing Core Data itself.

top_posts.title: How to Tile Images in SwiftUI
top_posts.summary: Image tiling in SwiftUI can be accomplished using different techniques. While the resizable modifier is the most common method, it has limitations like inability to adjust original image size or use specific parts of the image. A more intuitive and versatile method involves using foregroundStyle with ImagePaint, introduced in iOS 15. This allows for better control over image tiling. Additionally, custom images for tiling can be created using SwiftUI's GraphicsContext and Image constructors, especially useful for handling SF Symbols effectively across different iOS versions.

top_posts.summary: Starting with iOS 17, SwiftUI's new `scrollTargetBehavior` feature enhances scrolling control, allowing for custom implementations and precise view alignment. The post addresses limitations of default paging, offering step-by-step examples, and a refined method for implementing custom paging behaviors to resolve scrolling misalignment issues in landscape mode.

top_posts.title: Why Certain View Modifiers in Swift 6 Cannot Use the @State Property
top_posts.summary: Apple has enhanced SwiftUI’s performance with Xcode 16 under Swift 6 by making stricter concurrency checks. The `View` protocol is now comprehensively annotated with `@MainActor`, which can cause compile-time errors when using `@State` properties in certain view modifiers like `alignmentGuide`. The article explains the underlying reasons and provides solutions, such as using the underlying value of `State` directly or pre-fetching the `State` value outside the closure. These strategies help developers adapt to Swift 6 mode and deal with similar compile-time issues.
